benchmark.label: Benchmark (JNR)
benchmark.summary_md:
- **Approach:** non-parametric stratification by distance-to-forest-edge and subjurisdiction — the [JNR / riskmapjnr](https://ecology.ghislainv.fr/riskmapjnr/) baseline.
- **Training data:** dataset layers only (no point sample).
- **Output:** a vulnerability-class risk map, used as the baseline other models are compared against.
benchmark.description: The JNR Benchmark model implements the Jurisdictional and Nested REDD+ approach for deforestation risk mapping. It stratifies the landscape by distance-to-forest-edge bins and subjurisdictions, assigning historical deforestation rates as vulnerability scores. This non-parametric method requires no feature variables — it relies solely on spatial proximity to the forest edge. It serves as the baseline against which more complex models are compared.

blk_rows.label: Block rows
blk_rows.hint: Rows read per processing block — larger uses more memory, fewer I/O passes.

defor_threshold.label: Deforestation threshold (%)
defor_threshold.hint: Cumulative % of deforestation defining the max distance-to-edge kept (default 99.5).

forest_edge_var.label: Forest-edge variable
forest_edge_var.hint: Dataset layer giving distance to forest edge.

forest_var.label: Forest variable
forest_var.hint: Dataset layer with the forest mask (1 = forest).

subj_var.label: Subjurisdiction variable
subj_var.hint: Dataset layer of subjurisdiction zones used to stratify rates.

mw.label: Moving Window
mw.summary_md:
- **Approach:** local deforestation density in a sliding neighbourhood — spatial heuristic, no machine learning ([riskmapjnr](https://ecology.ghislainv.fr/riskmapjnr/)).
- **Training data:** dataset layers only (no point sample).
- **Output:** one risk raster per window size; smaller windows capture local detail, larger ones a broader trend.
mw.description: The Moving Window model computes local deforestation rates within spatial windows of specified sizes to produce risk rasters. For each window size, it calculates the proportion of deforested pixels in the neighbourhood, creating a spatial heuristic of event density. No machine learning is involved — the model captures local spatial patterns of forest loss. Multiple window sizes (e.g. 5, 11, 21 pixels) can be evaluated simultaneously.

win_size_list.label: Window sizes (px, comma-separated)
win_size_list.hint: Odd pixel sizes to evaluate, e.g. 5, 11, 21. Each produces its own risk map.

blk_rows.label: Block rows
blk_rows.hint: Rows read per processing block — larger uses more memory, fewer I/O passes.

defor_threshold.label: Deforestation threshold (%)
defor_threshold.hint: Cumulative % of deforestation defining the max distance-to-edge kept (default 99.5).

forest_edge_var.label: Forest-edge variable
forest_edge_var.hint: Dataset layer giving distance to forest edge.

forest_var.label: Forest variable
forest_var.hint: Dataset layer with the forest mask (1 = forest).

glm.label: GLM (Logistic Regression)
glm.summary_md:
- **Approach:** logistic regression — a linear, highly interpretable model ([scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression.html)).
- **Training data:** a point sample + the dataset's target and features.
- **Output:** deforestation-probability map plus per-feature coefficients quantifying each predictor's effect.
glm.description: The Generalized Linear Model uses logistic regression to estimate deforestation probability as a function of spatial predictor variables. It fits a linear combination of features (altitude, slope, distance to roads, etc.) through a logit link function. The model is fast to train, highly interpretable, and produces coefficient estimates that quantify each variable's contribution to deforestation risk. Uses sklearn's LogisticRegression with Patsy formula support.

solver.label: Solver
solver.hint: Optimisation algorithm sklearn uses to fit the coefficients. lbfgs suits most cases.

max_iter.label: Max iterations
max_iter.hint: Cap on solver iterations. Raise if the fit warns it did not converge.

rf.label: Random Forest
rf.summary_md:
- **Approach:** ensemble of decision trees — captures non-linear effects and interactions automatically ([scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier.html)).
- **Training data:** a point sample + the dataset's target and features.
- **Output:** deforestation-probability map plus feature-importance scores.
rf.description: The Random Forest model is an ensemble method that builds multiple decision trees on random subsets of training data and features. Each tree votes on whether a pixel is at risk of deforestation, and the ensemble averages these votes into a probability. It captures non-linear relationships and variable interactions without requiring explicit feature engineering. Feature importance scores help identify the most influential predictors.

n_trees.label: Number of trees
n_trees.hint: Trees in the ensemble — more is steadier but slower. 100–500 is typical.

max_depth.label: Max depth
max_depth.hint: Deepest a tree may grow. Lower guards against overfitting.

min_samples_leaf.label: Min samples per leaf
min_samples_leaf.hint: Fewest training points a leaf may hold. Higher smooths predictions.

random_seed.label: Random seed
random_seed.hint: Fixes reproducibility of the tree bootstrap and feature draws.

icar.label: iCAR (Bayesian Spatial)
icar.summary_md:
- **Approach:** Bayesian logistic model with a spatial random effect (rho) that absorbs unobserved neighbourhood structure — MCMC-fitted via [forestatrisk](https://ecology.ghislainv.fr/forestatrisk/).
- **Training data:** a point sample + the dataset's target and features.
- **Output:** deforestation-probability map plus an interpolated spatial random-effect (rho) raster. The most computationally intensive model, often the most accurate.
icar.description: The intrinsic Conditional Auto-Regressive (iCAR) model is a Bayesian spatial model that accounts for spatial autocorrelation through a latent random effect (rho). It combines the explanatory power of predictor variables with a spatial smoothing component that captures unobserved neighbourhood effects. Training uses Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling via the forestatrisk library. This is the most computationally intensive model but often yields the best spatial predictions.

csize.label: Cell size (km)
csize.hint: Side of the square cells used to build the spatial neighbourhood graph.

mcmc.label: MCMC iterations
mcmc.hint: Sampling iterations kept after burn-in — more improves the estimate but is slower.

burnin.label: Burn-in iterations
burnin.hint: Initial iterations discarded so the chain reaches its stationary distribution.

thin.label: Thinning factor
thin.hint: Keep every k-th sample to reduce autocorrelation. 1 keeps all.

prior_vrho.label: Prior variance (rho)
prior_vrho.hint: Prior variance of the spatial effect. -1 uses a uniform prior.

beta_start.label: Beta start
beta_start.hint: Starting value for the coefficients. -99 auto-initialises them.

random_seed.label: Random seed
random_seed.hint: Fixes reproducibility of the MCMC draws.

csize_interpolate.label: Interpolation cell size
csize_interpolate.hint: Cell size (km) the fitted rho is interpolated to for the output raster.
